summary: Learners formalise the everyday idea of an angle (a corner, a turn, an opening) as a geometric object: two rays (arms) sharing a common endpoint (the vertex), with size given by the amount of rotation or opening between the arms. The central challenge is that children hold SEPARATE angle ideas for different physical situations — the turn of a door, the corner of a shape, the opening of scissors, the slope of a ramp, a bend in a road — and must abstract the shared structure (two rays and a vertex) across all of them, including cases where one arm is only implicit (the horizontal in a slope or a sighting line). Suitable for roughly ages 9–10.
misconceptions: Holds separate, unconnected angle ideas for different contexts — a 'turn' and a 'corner' are treated as different things, with no single general concept
Judges or defines angle size by arm length or the distance between the arm-ends rather than the opening (persists even for doors and hinges)
Thinks the arms must be a fixed length, or that lengthening a ray changes the angle (arms are unbounded rays)
Only recognises an angle when both arms are drawn in a standard upright orientation — misses angles that are rotated or have an implicit arm (a slope)

activities.title: From many situations to one skeleton
steps: Gather or look at pictures of angles in many different situations: an open door, clock hands, open scissors, a propped ramp, a bent straw, a bend in a road, and the corner of a shape.
For each one, mark where the two arms are and put a dot on the vertex (the meeting point), drawing an arc at the vertex to show the angle.
Strip each situation down to the SAME bare diagram — two rays meeting at a point with an arc — and lay these stripped diagrams side by side.
Say in your own words what the door, the clock and the scissors all share.
For the ramp, draw in the implicit second arm (the horizontal ground line) so the angle has both arms.
activities.insight: A door, a clock and a pair of scissors are all the same underlying thing — two arms meeting at a point — so an angle is that shared skeleton, not any one particular picture. Some situations (slopes, sightings) have one arm that must be drawn in.

activities.title: The arms are rays: lengthening does not change the angle
steps: Draw an angle, then predict (before doing anything) what will happen to the angle if you extend both arms to twice their length, and say why.
Now extend both arms — or slide an identical angle with longer arms on top, with the vertices aligned — and compare.
Describe what you notice: the longer arms lie along the same two lines, so the opening is unchanged.
Compare two angles that have the same opening but different arm lengths and decide whether they are equal, giving your reason.
activities.insight: The arms of an angle are rays that can be extended without changing the angle; the size is the opening (the turn) between the arms, not how long the arms are or how far apart the arm-ends sit.

activities.title: Connecting the corner and the turn
steps: Take one object, such as an open door or a pair of scissors, and look at it as a static corner: two lines meeting at a point.
Now open and close it, watching the arms sweep through a turn, and notice the amount of turn is the size of the angle.
Explain how the still corner and the turning action describe the same angle on the same object.
Use a clock face: point to the vertex (the centre) and name the two hands as the two arms, then describe the angle as the turn between them.
activities.insight: An angle has two connected conceptions — a static corner (two arms at a vertex) and a dynamic turn (an amount of rotation) — and these describe the same geometric object.

activities.title: Is it an angle? Including rotated and implicit-arm cases
steps: Look at a set of pictures: a clearly drawn angle, an angle rotated off the upright, a ramp with only its slope line drawn, and two parallel lines that never meet.
For each picture, decide whether there is an angle and, if so, mark the vertex.
For the ramp, draw in the implicit horizontal arm and decide whether there is an angle there.
Say why the parallel lines do NOT form an angle (they never meet, so there is no vertex).
Explain in your own words what makes something an angle.
activities.insight: An angle is two rays meeting at a vertex, recognisable even when rotated or when one arm is implicit; two lines that never meet do not form an angle because there is no shared vertex.

checkQuestion: Lay out several pictures: a clearly drawn angle, a rotated angle, a ramp with only its slope line drawn, and a non-angle (two parallel lines that never meet). Say: 'Point to the angle in each picture and mark its vertex — and for the ramp, tell me if there's an angle there at all.' Then: 'Explain what makes something an angle.'
checkAnswer: Identifies angles including the rotated one and the ramp (recognising the implicit horizontal as the second arm), marks the vertex where the two rays meet, rejects the parallel-lines non-angle, and justifies that an angle is two rays/arms meeting at a point (a vertex) with its size the turn or opening between them.
